headline: Ancient Food Tradition Holds Key to Zambia's Food Security
meta_description: Research shows edible insects could strengthen food security in rural Zambia, but the tradition needs community support and proper integration into mainstream…
summary_short: A new study reveals how reviving Zambia's centuries-old practice of eating insects could tackle food insecurity—if communities embrace it.
body:
In rural Zambia's Central province, researchers have discovered an unexpected path toward stronger food security: rediscovering what local communities have known for generations. A study by John Nyawali and Jasper Knight from the University of the Witwatersrand surveyed 139 households and found that edible insects already contribute meaningfully to nutrition and household food security. The practice of entomophagy—eating insects as food—is deeply rooted in Zambian culture, yet it has faded in recent years, particularly among younger generations. The researchers believe that reversing this decline could offer substantial benefits, though success will depend on how mainstream society embraces the practice.

One surprising finding emerged: households with higher education levels actually consumed more insects than those with less education, challenging the false narrative that insect-eating signifies poverty or primitiveness. This suggests educated community leaders could become powerful advocates for entomophagy by highlighting its economic and nutritional value. Co-author Knight emphasized that connecting insect consumption to existing public health programs—such as maternal and child health care and school nutrition initiatives—could naturally integrate insects back into community diets.

The path forward requires careful balance. Researchers stress that insect farming should remain small-scale and community-controlled, allowing rural families to develop sustainable incomes without being displaced by large agribusinesses. As Knight noted simply: "Insects are healthy, nutritious and free." Yet broader adoption may require some commercialization, a tension experts continue to debate. What's clear is that Zambia's edible insect tradition represents an underutilized resource—one that nourished communities for centuries and could help secure food systems for generations to come.
quick_facts: 139 rural households surveyed in Zambia's Central province
Edible insects decline in popularity, especially among young people
Educated households consume more insects than less-educated ones
Insects are free and highly nutritious food source
Small-scale farming preferred over large agribusiness operations
